definitions.definition: On ℝ^n and ℝ^m use the standard Euclidean inner product v·w=∑_k v_k w_k and norm |v|=(v·v)^(1/2). Spatial Lebesgue measure dx is the product of the n ordinary one-dimensional Lebesgue measures in the standard coordinates. For any function on ℝ^n×(0,∞), ∂_{x_j} means its componentwise derivative in spatial coordinate j (1≤j≤n), and ∂_t its componentwise time derivative, where these derivatives exist. In particular u_t=∂_t u, u_tt=∂_t(∂_t u), and ∂_{x_jx_j}u=∂_{x_j}(∂_{x_j}u). For scalar functions the same conventions apply. D_xu denotes the matrix with columns ∂_{x_j}u, and its squared Frobenius norm is ∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|². Smooth means derivatives of every finite order exist and are continuous on the stated open domain. An integral without a displayed measure is the Lebesgue integral; integrable means measurable with finite integral of the absolute value (or norm).

For every t>0, e(·,t) is integrable. More precisely, for each t0>0 there exist a compact C⊂ℝ^n, R>0 and B≥0 such that, writing J=[t0/2,3t0/2] and Q=[−R,R]^n, one has C⊂(−R,R)^n, u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J, and all positive-order derivatives of u vanish for x∉C and r∈int J. The box Q has Lebesgue measure (2R)^n<∞. For every r∈int J, each of the spatial functions e, e_t, u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_j}u, and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), evaluated at time r, is continuous, vanishes outside C, and is integrable on ℝ^n, for each 1≤j≤n. Finally |e_t(x,r)|≤B for all (x,r)∈Q×[3t0/4,5t0/4].

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and an index 1≤j≤n. Choose compatible C,R from N002 and put Q=[−R,R]^n and g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). H002 makes g smooth. N002 gives g=0 off C and C⊂int Q, so g vanishes on a neighborhood of the boundary of Q (the open complement of C contains that boundary). Apply M007 along the jth coordinate to u_t and ∂_{x_j}u at time t0. This gives ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u. Each term is continuous and integrable by N002.

produces.statement: g is smooth, zero near ∂Q, and ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t(·,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(·,t0)+u_t(·,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(·,t0). All three functions in this equality are integrable and vanish outside C.

argument.text: For each fixed choice of the remaining n−1 coordinates in [−R,R], consider the scalar function of x_j obtained by restricting g to that coordinate line. It is smooth on ℝ, including both endpoints −R and R. Its derivative is continuous and hence integrable on this compact interval, and the function has zero value at both endpoints because these points lie on the boundary of Q, outside C. M002 therefore gives ∫_{−R}^{R} ∂_{x_j}g dx_j=0. To make the product identification explicit, define split(x)=(x_j,(x_k)_{k≠j}) with the other coordinates ordered increasingly. Insertion at position j is its inverse, as is checked coordinate by coordinate. Since 1≤j≤n, one has n=(n−1)+1. Apply M010 with d=n−1, every coordinate space ℝ, every coordinate measure the Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R], and selected index j (converted to zero-based Fin n). Each coordinate measure is finite, hence sigma-finite. The source gives that split is a measure-preserving measurable equivalence between Lebesgue measure restricted to Q and the product of the jth restricted coordinate measure with the restricted product of the other coordinates; the original product of restrictions is the restriction of dx to Q because both agree on coordinate rectangles. Thus transport by split takes the integrable function ∂_{x_j}g on Q to its composition with insertion, with the same integral and integrability for this product measure. Now M003 integrates the selected first factor in the inner integral. The FTC equality just proved makes that inner integral zero at every choice of the remaining coordinates in their box. Hence ∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=0. When n=1 the remaining coordinate space is a singleton with empty product measure of mass one, so the same argument reduces to the FTC equality. Endpoints do not affect the Lebesgue interval integral since singletons have zero measure.

All terms of F001 vanish outside Q by N002, since C⊂int Q. Thus their integrals over Q equal their whole-space integrals. Integrate the equality in F001 and use F002 and linearity for the integrable summands: 0=∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u dx+∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. Symmetry of the real dot product and subtraction give precisely the asserted integration-by-parts identity, including finiteness of both sides. Since t0 and j were arbitrary this proves the output.
